reward_note: Credit applied to your energy consumption, not money in your pocket. It is a simulated bill credit for this demonstration and cannot be withdrawn as cash.

lessons.title: Follow the energy
lessons.summary: Where your solar power goes, in three taps.

steps.title: Your panels make it
steps.text: Sunlight on your panels becomes electricity. The amount changes through the day: low in the morning, highest around midday, zero at night.

steps.title: Your building uses it first
steps.text: Whatever is running right now (fridge, lights, oven) takes solar power first. That part never touches your bill.

steps.title: The grid balances the rest
steps.text: Extra solar is exported to the grid. When you need more than the panels give, the grid supplies the difference. That is import.

lessons.example: 4.8 kW from the panels and 1.6 kW used inside leaves 3.2 kW exported.

questions.text: Your panels produce 5 kW and you are using 2 kW. What happens to the other 3 kW?
options: It is exported to the grid
It is imported from the grid

questions.text: At night your panels produce nothing. Where does your electricity come from (with no battery)?

lessons.title: kW and kWh without the headache
lessons.summary: Speed versus distance, but for electricity.

steps.title: kW is how fast
steps.text: Kilowatts (kW) tell you how much power is flowing right now, like the speed on a car's dashboard.

steps.title: kWh is how much
steps.text: Kilowatt-hours (kWh) tell you how much energy was used or produced over time, like the distance you drove. Your bill counts kWh.

steps.title: Multiply to convert
steps.text: Power multiplied by time gives energy. A 2 kW oven running for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.

lessons.example: A big-screen TV draws about 0.1 kW, so 1 kWh runs it for roughly 10 hours.

questions.text: A 1 kW heater runs for 4 hours. How much energy does it use?
Which unit does your electricity bill charge for?

lessons.title: Give sunshine a time slot
lessons.summary: Why timing a task can lower your bill.

steps.title: Exported energy earns less
steps.text: In most contracts the price you receive for exported energy is lower than the price you pay to import it.

steps.title: So use your own solar
steps.text: Running a flexible task (dishwasher, washing, EV charging) while the sun is shining uses energy you would otherwise export cheaply.

steps.title: The benefit is the difference
steps.text: For every kWh you move into a sunny window you avoid the import price and give up the export price. The gap between them is what you keep.

lessons.example: Import 1.30 RON/kWh and export 0.55 RON/kWh: moving 6 kWh into solar hours is worth about 6 × 0.75 = 4.50 RON.

questions.text: When is the best time to run a flexible appliance if you have solar panels?
options: While the panels are producing a surplus

questions.text: Import costs 1.20 RON/kWh and export pays 0.50 RON/kWh. What is each shifted kWh worth?

lessons.title: Stay safe, get the right help
lessons.summary: What to do when something looks wrong.

steps.title: Danger comes first
steps.text: Smoke, fire, burning smells or sparks are emergencies. Move away and call the emergency services. Do not wait for an app.

steps.title: Look, do not touch
steps.text: Never open the inverter, touch damaged cables or climb onto the roof to inspect panels. Describe what you can see from a safe place.

steps.title: One request, the right team
steps.text: Choose the closest request type in Support. Production issues go to solar maintenance, billing questions go to your supplier, and unclear cases are reviewed by a person.

lessons.example: "Production dropped since Tuesday and the display shows a warning" is a perfect support request.

questions.text: You smell burning near the inverter. What do you do first?
options: Move away and call the emergency services
Send a support request and wait

questions.text: Your production looks lower than usual. What is a safe way to help the technician?
options: Climb onto the roof to inspect the panels
Describe what you see from a safe place
